evidence.s1_requirements: Every point in steps/1.md is met. `snapshot()` returns `{version, root}` with only primitives, arrays and plain objects (step1.patch src/BehaviourTree.ts L1942-1944). `BehaviourTreeSnapshot` is exported from src/index.ts (L2151). `restore()` validates the whole snapshot before applying it (L1951-1967). Every piece of state the step lists is kept: node states, composite children, repeat/retry target and current counts (Repeat.ts/Retry.ts getSnapshot), the lotto child as an index (Lotto.ts L2298-2303), and the wait's total and waited durations (Wait.ts L2664-2678). For a restored wait the agent rebases `initialUpdateTime = now - waitedDuration` in clock mode and keeps `waitedDuration` in getDeltaTime mode, so time between snapshot and restore does not count. A finished tree restores as finished, and BehaviourTree.step's existing reset starts a new run that makes its random choices again. The README has a `snapshot()`/`restore(snapshot)` section with a workflow example (step1.patch README L17-76). No requirement is unmet.
evidence.s1_correctness: Each node type that holds private state saves it. I grepped src/nodes for private fields: only Action, Lotto, Repeat, Retry and Wait have execution state, and each overrides getSnapshot, validateSnapshot and restoreSnapshot. Sequence, selector, parallel, race and all keep no index, so the state of their children is enough. restoreSnapshot assigns `_state` directly (Node.ts L2202-2204), so no callbacks fire. Action now tracks the identity of its pending promise (`this.updatePromise !== updatePromise`, Action.ts L2541/2552), so a promise from before a restore that settles later is ignored. That is a correctness fix that was needed and easy to miss. A running lotto with no picked child is rejected, and a guard-resolved lotto with no pick is accepted (Lotto.ts L2314-2321). A wait taken while waiting on the clock counts the time since its last step (Wait.ts L2667-2670). Infinite delta times are clamped so the snapshot survives JSON. The test harness `assertRestoredTreeBehavesLikeOriginal` (test L97-159) compares node states, the agent call log and the result for every snapshot point. It covers composites, decorators, conditions, callbacks, while/until guards, subtrees, random counts, both time modes and finished trees.
evidence.s2_validation: The snapshot now carries a fingerprint of the definition: a cyrb53 hash of a canonicalised JSON form. Keys are sorted, the defaults the MDSL parser always adds (`args: []`, `succeedOnAbort: false`) are dropped, and named roots are sorted by id (step2.patch BehaviourTreeDefinitionUtilities.ts L467-523). I checked MDSLDefinitionParser.ts L653-695: those are the only defaults the parser adds. A mismatch throws 'invalid snapshot: snapshot does not match the tree's definition' (BehaviourTree.ts L444-446). Arrays are now rejected along with null and non-objects, and a missing version, fingerprint or root is rejected. All checks run before anything is mutated. Tests assert that the tree is unchanged after a rejected restore, both its node states and its snapshot, and that it keeps behaving like a control tree (test L1633-1693). An MDSL/JSON accept matrix of 4x4 variants is at L1696-1807, and ten 'different definition' cases are rejected (L1575-1631). A pending action is saved as READY with no result (Action.ts L565). The README documents that it is called again, along with its entry callback (step2.patch README L32-37).
evidence.s3_fixes: Neither reported bug reproduces in the step-2 code. restoreSnapshot never calls setState, and every getSnapshot builds fresh objects; Action's restore copies `{ ...updatePromiseResult }`. So step 3 adds only regression tests (step3.patch, one commit 07bea11) and makes no src changes. That is reasonable, and it is honest not to invent fixes. The tests check that restore never calls onNodeStateChange: snapshots taken after 0-14 steps, restored into trees already stepped 0 or 5 times (L38-60). They check that the next step reports changes as usual (L62-83). They check that a snapshot is not changed by stepping the source or the restored tree, and equals a snapshot taken right after restore, in both time modes and with promise-based actions (L86-226). One gap: the clock-mode case fakes `Date` and never ticks between `restore` and `snapshot` (L102, L160-173). Wait.getSnapshot computes the waited time from the live clock, so with a real clock a snapshot taken any milliseconds after `restore(s)` will not equal `s` for a running wait. The tests hide this, and it is neither discussed nor documented.
evidence.design: Each node class owns its state through getSnapshot, validateSnapshot and restoreSnapshot overrides that chain to super (Composite and Decorator recurse into children). The public surface is small: `snapshot()`, `restore(snapshot: BehaviourTreeSnapshot)` and one exported type, built as a discriminated union per node type in a new src/BehaviourTreeSnapshot.ts. It follows the repository's style: JSDoc on every member and lowercase error messages. Weaknesses: every getSnapshot ends in a cast (`as NodeSnapshot`, e.g. Node.ts L2173 and Lotto.ts L2302), which gives up the union's type checking. `isNonNegativeInteger` is added to Utilities.ts while BehaviourTreeDefinitionUtilities already has `isInteger`. A hand-rolled hash adds about 30 lines to the utilities file. The Action change to track promise identity is minimal and needed.
evidence.tests: All tests are in one new file, test/BehaviourTreeSnapshot.spec.ts, using mocha, chai's assert and sinon fake timers like the existing tests. It has a generic harness that compares a restored tree against the original at every step point, plus targeted tests for: the JSON round trip, rewinding the same instance, repeat and retry counts including random ones, lotto picks including the guard-resolved case, waits in both time modes including 'hours pass before restore', infinite delta time, promise results that settled but were not yet handled (resolved, rejected, invalid), pending promises, finished trees and re-randomisation, and validation of every field. Step 2 removed one step-1 test, 'cannot be taken while the promise has not settled' (step2.patch L628). The behaviour it tested was intentionally replaced, and new tests cover the replacement. No baseline test was touched. The one weakness is the frozen clock in the step-3 equality test.
evidence.docs: The README adds a feature bullet, `snapshot()` and `restore(snapshot)` sections, a realistic persistence example, and a 'Snapshots and Promise-based Actions' subsection. In step 2 that subsection states plainly that a pending action is restored as READY and its function and entry callback are called again (step2.patch README L32-37). It also documents the definition-matching rules, including that registered subtrees and functions are not covered (L22). package.json and package-lock.json are bumped from 4.3.1 to 4.4.0, a minor bump for a feature. The Version History table gets a 4.4.0 row, and step 2 adds continuation rows in the same multi-row style as 4.3.0. That is right, since 4.4.0 was not yet released.
evidence.process: There are 13 commits with conventional, descriptive messages. Features are split by concern: node states, repeat/retry, lotto, wait, settled promises, then docs and version. Generated dist rebuilds have their own chore commits, which fits since dist/ is tracked in the baseline. Steps 2 and 3 each have small focused commits. Two step-1 commits touch a planning spec ('docs: spec for tree snapshot and restore', 'docs: mark snapshot spec as done ...') that does not appear in app/ or in the patches, so I cannot judge its content. No dependencies were added, and nothing beyond the steps was implemented.

unmet_requirements: Step 3 report 2, partly: in clock mode, a snapshot taken after `restore(s)` and before any step equals `s` only if no milliseconds pass, because Wait.getSnapshot reads the live clock. The regression test freezes `Date`, which hides this.
strengths: Snapshot and restore are correct across every node type, with real attention to subtle cases: tracking promise identity so a promise from before a restore that settles later is ignored, guard-resolved lotto nodes, time between the last step and the snapshot in clock mode, and infinite delta times.

Validation is complete and atomic. A canonicalised definition fingerprint accepts MDSL and equivalent JSON (including reordered properties and named roots) and rejects real differences with the required message, and a rejected restore leaves the tree untouched.

The tests are very thorough: a generic harness checks at every step point that the restored tree matches the original in node states, agent call order and result, alongside targeted edge-case and validation tests.
issues: The step-3 regression test for 'a snapshot right after restore equals s' runs with `Date` frozen. With a real clock, a running wait's waited time grows between `restore` and `snapshot`, so the equality the report asks for is not guaranteed, and this is neither discussed nor documented.
Every getSnapshot override is cast with `as NodeSnapshot`, which discards the type checking the discriminated union could give.

There is minor duplication and extra code: `isNonNegativeInteger` is added to Utilities.ts next to the existing `isInteger` in BehaviourTreeDefinitionUtilities, and a hand-written cyrb53 hash is added for the fingerprint.
review.verdict: This is a careful, well-tested and well-documented implementation that meets nearly every requirement of all three steps, and in step 3 it correctly found that neither reported bug reproduced. I would merge it after one follow-up: make or document a clear decision on the clock-mode waited time, so that a snapshot taken right after restore reliably equals the restored snapshot, and test it with a clock that moves.
